item.title: Is President Sahabuddin leaving office?
item.description:
President Mohammed Shahabuddin is expected to resign from office, citing health concerns, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter, although no formal resignation letter has yet been submitted.
Several sources said the BNP government has agreed in principle to the move following discussions with the president. They added that Shahabuddin intends to travel to a Southeast Asian island nation after stepping down.
President's Press Secretary Mohammad Sarwar Alam confirmed to a national media outlet that Shahabuddin had expressed his intention to resign and that the government had agreed to the proposal.
The development comes as Speaker of Parliament Hafiz Uddin Ahmad has cut short his visit to Thailand and is returning to Bangladesh earlier than scheduled.
Sources at the Parliament Secretariat said the Speaker had been requested by senior government officials to return as soon as possible to complete the constitutional process required for the president's resignation.
Hafiz travelled to Bangkok on July 19 for medical treatment and was originally scheduled to return on July 26.
However, Parliament Secretariat Director (Public Relations-1) Mohammad Monir Hossain confirmed to Dhaka Tribune on Thursday night that the Speaker will return on Friday.
Under Article 50 of the Constitution, the president may resign by submitting a written letter to the Speaker of Parliament.
Article 54 states that if the office of the president becomes vacant or the president is unable to perform the duties of the office, the Speaker assumes the role of acting president until a new president is elected.
Hence, if Shahabuddin resigns, Hafiz Uddin Ahmad would become acting president.
The last acting president in Bangladesh was the late Jamir Uddin Sircar, who was speaker of the Eighth Parliament.
He assumed the role of acting president in 2002 after the resignation of former president AQM Badruddoza Chowdhury during the BNP-Jamaat-led four-party alliance government.
Jamir Uddin Sircar served as acting president for 78 days, from June 21 to September 6, 2002
According to multiple sources, the president has made a policy-level decision to resign, but the formal submission of his resignation letter is reportedly being delayed because the Speaker of Parliament is currently abroad.
A source close to the president said he recently told several officials in his office: "I may wrap up my time at Bangabhaban within the next couple of days."
Since then, discussions about his possible resignation have become more intense.
A senior Bangabhaban official said: "The president cannot resign immediately because, under the Constitution, the resignation letter must be submitted to the Speaker. Since the Speaker is currently outside the country, that is not possible at the moment."
The official added that the president has already decided to resign, whether for health reasons or mental stress.
On Thursday, Md Nurul Amin, secretary to the president, said: "The president has not yet signed a resignation letter. If he resigns, it will be announced."
As a result, the president's Office has neither confirmed nor directly denied the reports.
Multiple BNP sources claim that senior party leaders have conveyed to President Shahabuddin, who was elected during the Awami League government's tenure, that he should step down.
The president’s office added political significance, as the next president's term will cover the period during which Bangladesh's 14th parliamentary election is due to be held by 2031.
Discussions are also reportedly taking place within policymaking circles regarding a possible successor as multiple senior politicians and two bureaucrats' names are in the discussion.
However, the ruling party BNP will select its candidate, and it will be passed, maintaining the constitutional procedure.
Responding to journalists at the Secretariat on Thursday, Salahuddin Ahmed said: "Rumors about the president's resignation remain just rumors. If it actually happens, we will respond accordingly. If the president wishes to step down for health or other reasons, the Constitution provides for that. However, I have no information confirming his resignation."
The home minister also said: “The government has taken no action regarding this matter, nor is it making any official statement. Whether the president wants to resign for health reasons is something that should be asked of him.”
When asked about media reports claiming that President Shahabuddin spoke by telephone with former prime minister Sheikh Hasina while receiving medical treatment in London in May this year, the home minister said he had no knowledge of the matter.
Under Article 123 of the Constitution, a new president must be elected by members of parliament within 90 days of the office becoming vacant.
Since the BNP currently holds a majority in Parliament, its nominated candidate would be expected to win the presidential election if the office becomes vacant.
The next president is also expected to serve during Bangladesh's next parliamentary election, making the appointment politically significant as well as constitutionally important.
Following the 2024 mass uprising, several student organizations and leaders of the July movement demanded President Shahabuddin's resignation.
They organized demonstrations, including protests outside Bangabhaban. However, the interim government did not remove him.
Even after the BNP later formed the government, no immediate action was taken.
Mohammed Shahabuddin was sworn in as Bangladesh's 22nd President on 24 April 2023, having been nominated by the Awami League, whose acitivities have been banned.
Under the Constitution, his five-year term is scheduled to end in April 2028.

item.title: Speaker likely to return early from Thailand amid speculation over President's resignation
item.description:
Hafiz Uddin Ahmad Bir Bikram is likely to return home on Friday after cutting short his overseas visit to Thailand amid growing speculation over the resignation of President Mohammed Shahabuddin.
“The Speaker is likely to return home on Friday instead of Sunday next,” BNP's Media Cell member Shairul Kabir Khan said on Thursday.
He said the Speaker left for Thailand on July 19 for medical treatment. “Although his return is originally scheduled for July 26, he is now expected to arrive in Dhaka at 12:40pm on July 24,” he added.
The Speaker's early return comes amid widespread speculation over the possible resignation of President Shahabuddin, although there has been no official confirmation from Bangabhaban, the government or the ruling party.
Under Article 54 of the Constitution, if the office of the President falls vacant, the Speaker assumes the responsibilities of the President until a new one is elected.
As per the Constitution, if the President wants to resign, he needs to send a resignation letter to the Speaker.
If the President steps down, the Speaker shall take charge of acting President until the election of the next President.
As per Article 123(2) of the Constitution, a new President must be elected within 90 days of the office falling vacant due to death, resignation or removal, while Article 48(1) provides for the President's election through a vote by the members of parliament.
Shahabuddin took office on April 24, 2023, for a five-year term. However, speculation has intensified in recent days that he may resign before completing his tenure.

item.title: Trump says Saudi nuclear deal contingent on recognizing Israel
item.description:
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that a deal with Saudi Arabia to establish a civilian nuclear program would be contingent on the kingdom’s recognition of Israel, a move long sought by Washington but resisted by Riyadh.
The announcements came as the United States fights a war with Iran that began in large part over concerns about Tehran’s nuclear program.
Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said recognition by Saudi Arabia, a regional power and home to Islam’s holiest sites, would mark a “historic leap” forward for peace in the Middle East.
Saudi Arabia has resisted a concerted push by the US to join the so-called Abraham Accords with Israel, insisting on a pathway to a Palestinian state before it offers recognition.
The deal announced Wednesday to establish a civilian nuclear program in the Gulf kingdom “will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords,” Trump said.
Should it go through, the deal would generate billions of dollars for American companies and would be a major win for Saudi Arabia on both the economic and diplomatic fronts.
But with Trump’s latest announcement, it was unclear whether the deal would ever see the light of day.
If Washington “tries to force normalization on Riyadh, it’s not likely to work out very well,” said HA Hellyer, senior associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute for Defense and Security Studies.
“Would Saudi decide to do a complete 180 on what it has declared for the past three years, or 30 years? Quite dubious,” he told AFP.
And if it does go through, critics have insisted the deal -- the text of which was not immediately made public -- could precipitate a nuclear race in a region already battered by war.
One provision would potentially see US companies build a uranium enrichment facility in Saudi Arabia, the Wall Street Journal reported.
The US Energy Department made no mention of such a provision and did not offer comment when asked about it by AFP, while Trump added in his Truth Social post that “there will be no enrichment of material!”
The deal will be submitted to Congress for review.
US lawmakers from both parties and Israeli officials have previously voiced opposition to such a project over fears Saudi Arabia could eventually convert it to develop nuclear weapons.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that “any agreement that we’re going to make with any country in the world on civil nuclear energy is going to be one that will have safeguards in place to ensure that it can’t be turned into a weapons program.”
Riyadh, like Tehran, has long been adamant about its right to pursue a civilian nuclear program. Last year it signed a mutual defense pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan.
Policymakers have long feared that if Iran produced a nuclear weapon, the move would set off an arms race across the Gulf.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright dismissed concerns about proliferation, insisting the deal was in Washington’s economic and strategic interest.
“These agreements uphold the highest standards of nuclear safety and nonproliferation, while relying on the world’s best nuclear technology and scientists, designed right here in the United States,” he said.
The United States has agreements governing nuclear cooperation with more than 50 countries.
Experts said such a deal had been in the works for a while, but some raised concerns about the potential for uranium enrichment on Saudi soil.
“It would be a mistake to allow Saudi Arabia the capability for enrichment,” Matthew Kroenig of the Atlantic Council said before the deal was formally announced.
“Washington is right to strengthen its relationship with Riyadh, but it should not do so at the expense of its effective nuclear weapons nonproliferation standards.”

item.title: Students absent on July 13 HSC tests allowed retake
item.description:
Students who could not sit for the Physics, Accounting and Logic examinations on July 13 due to floods will be allowed to take the tests again after registration, Education Minister ANM Ehsanul Haque Milon said on Thursday.
The minister said the examinations held on July 13 will be rescheduled, but only those students who were absent on that day will be eligible to participate.
Speaking to reporters on Thursday afternoon, he said there would be no opportunity for students who already appeared in the examinations but want to retake them due to poor performance.
“No, no. That is not possible. Those who have already taken the exams will not have to sit again,” the minister said.
He added that marks would be awarded to all students for questions that contained errors, leaving no further scope for complaints.
The HSC and equivalent examinations were held on July 13 in 59 districts across the country, excluding five districts of Chittagong. The decision to hold the exams amid heavy rainfall and waterlogging sparked widespread dissatisfaction among examinees.
On July 14, students staged protests across the country demanding a reconsideration of the examination schedule.

item.title: Mozaffar shown arrested in crimes against humanity case
item.description:
The International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) on Thursday ordered that Major (retd) Mozaffar Hossain, one of the prime accused in the former president Ziaur Rahman assassination case, to be shown arrested in a case over crimes against humanity committed in Feni during the July 2024 uprising.
The three-member ICT-2, chaired by Justice Nazrul Islam Chowdhury, also granted the prosecution two days to interrogate the accused.
It fixed September 23 for submission of the investigation report.
The other members of the tribunal are Judge Md Manjurul Bashid and Judge Nur Mohammad Shahriar Kabir.
Chief Prosecutor Md Aminul Islam represented the prosecution during the hearing.
Earlier in the day, Mozaffar was produced before the tribunal. He will remain in Dhaka Cantonment Jail.
The Detective Branch (DB) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) arrested Mozaffar in the capital on July 15 after over 45 years on the run.
Later, he was handed over to the Military Police at Dhaka Cantonment as his trial in the Zia assassination case will be held under the military law.
Meanwhile, another accused in the crimes against humanity case, Lieutenant General (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury, was also produced before the tribunal.

item.title: Experts push Volunteer Peer Leader model for adolescent health
item.description:
A national consultation recommended institutionalizing the Volunteer Peer Leader (VPL) Model within Adolescent-Friendly Health Centers (AFHCs) to improve adolescents' access to inclusive, youth-friendly health services, particularly mental health support.
The consultation, organized by SERAC-Bangladesh, brought together policymakers, public health experts, development partners, youth representatives and government officials to discuss integrating the model into the country's public health system.
The meeting was chaired by Dr Syed Kamrul Islam, director (PHC & ITHC) at the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) and chair of the Technical Working Group.
In his welcome remarks, SM Shaikat, executive director of SERAC-Bangladesh, said: "The Volunteer Peer Leader Model offers an effective solution to the human resource shortages in health facilities."
He said trained Volunteer Peer Leaders provide basic counseling, essential adolescent health information and referral support, serving as a bridge between communities and health facilities through a government-approved training curriculum.
Md Nazmul Hasan, project manager of SERAC-Bangladesh, presented the rationale for the VPL Model, its key interventions and gaps in adolescent health services. He said the model improves adolescents' access to health information, basic counseling, referral services and adolescent-friendly healthcare.
During the discussion, participants said institutionalizing the model would require a clear implementation framework, well-defined terms of reference, policy endorsement and adequate financial planning.
They also noted that many adolescents remain reluctant to seek healthcare because of social and cultural barriers, adding that trained Volunteer Peer Leaders can provide counseling, health education, awareness and referrals while strengthening links between communities and health facilities.
Participants said initiatives are underway to establish Adolescent Focal Bodies at the upazila and district levels in line with the National Adolescent Health Strategy.
They added that integrating the VPL Model into this structure, supported by standardized training packages, implementation guidelines, policy briefs and financial analysis, would facilitate its adoption within the government health system. Gradual expansion of the model across all upazilas, they said, could improve adolescents' access to inclusive and adolescent-friendly health services.
Sharing field experiences, Volunteer Peer Leader Md Boni Amin from Barguna said VPLs receive foundation training on the National Adolescent Health Strategy, adolescent development, communication skills and group facilitation before conducting awareness sessions in schools and communities, encouraging adolescents to seek healthcare and facilitating referrals to health facilities.
The consultation was attended by senior officials from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, DGHS, the Directorate General of Family Planning (DGFP), development partners, academics, members of the Technical Working Group, Volunteer Peer Leaders, representatives of government and nongovernment organizations, and members of the national media.

item.title: Women are ready to lead, but are workplaces ready to share power?
item.description:
Bangladesh has expanded girls' education, increased women's participation in the workforce, and seen women emerge as leaders in different sectors. Yet women remain strikingly absent from leadership positions—not because they lack talent, but because structural barriers continue to hold them back, speakers at a roundtable in Dhaka said.
The discussion, titled "Rise & Lead: Breaking Barriers, Sharing Power and Advancing Women's Leadership in Bangladesh," held on Thursday, brought together dozens of policymakers, academics, business leaders and development practitioners to examine why women continue to struggle to reach decision-making roles despite decades of progress.
Organised by Oxfam in Bangladesh and Dhaka Tribune under the Onirban–Rise & Lead programme, the event argued that unequal opportunities, discriminatory workplace cultures, inflexible employment practices and the unequal burden of unpaid care work continue to prevent women from advancing into leadership.
State Minister for Women and Children Affairs and Social Welfare Barrister Farzana Sharmin Putul, the chief guest, said changing laws alone would not be enough.
"Leadership is not a position or title; it is a state of mind. Sustainable development cannot be achieved through laws and institutions alone unless society changes the way it thinks about leadership and equality."
She urged schools and universities to cultivate leadership, self-awareness and mental well-being from an early age, while reaffirming the government's commitment to working with organisations promoting women's leadership.
Presenting findings from the Rise & Lead programme under the theme "Women are ready to lead: Are our workplaces ready to share power?", Mahmuda Sultana, programme director at Oxfam in Bangladesh, and Uma Chatterjee, facilitator at Leadership Lab, Change Mantras, said Bangladesh's economic progress has not translated into equal leadership opportunities for women.
Mahmuda Sultana said many women never reach leadership positions not because they lack competence, but because the system is stacked against them.
"Many capable women are constrained not by a lack of skills but by unequal opportunities, limited confidence and workplace environments that fail to support their growth."
Presenting the programme findings alongside Uma Chatterjee, facilitator at Leadership Lab, Change Mantras, she argued that Bangladesh's economic gains have not translated into equal leadership opportunities for women.
According to World Bank 2025 ILO-modelled estimates presented at the event, women's labour force participation stands at 38.6%, compared with 80.4% for men. The Bangladesh Labour Force Survey 2022 estimated women's participation at 42.8%.
The findings also showed that 96.6% of employed women work in the informal sector, where job security, social protection and career advancement remain limited. Women also perform more than seven times as much unpaid care and domestic work as men, leaving them with less time and fewer opportunities to build careers that lead to leadership.
The programme identified multiple barriers keeping women from senior positions, including discriminatory workplace practices, inflexible work arrangements, unsafe working environments, limited access to mentors and professional networks, stigma surrounding career breaks, unequal distribution of authority and persistent self-doubt reinforced by years of exclusion.
Opening the discussion, Dhaka Tribune News Editor Anando Mostofa said women have repeatedly proved their capabilities across every sector, yet remain underrepresented in leadership because of structural and social barriers rather than a lack of ability.
"The time for debating women's leadership has passed. What we need now is a workplace where opportunities are defined by merit and ability, not gender."
Md. Sariful Islam, Head of Influencing, Communications, Advocacy and Media at Oxfam in Bangladesh, moderated the discussion. Roop Sen, facilitator at Change Mantras, also participated in the event.
The Rise & Lead initiative aims to make women's leadership, career reintegration and workplace progression national priorities while encouraging employers, policymakers and development partners to build more inclusive institutions and expand women's participation in decision-making.

item.title: Passenger held with 720g gold at Shahjalal airport
item.description:
Intelligence officials have detained a passenger at the domestic terminal of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport after recovering 720 grams (about 61 bhori) of gold concealed in a special compartment.
The suspect was detained around 12pm on Thursday and later handed over to the Airport Police Station, Officer-in-Charge (OC) Kamrul Islam Talukder confirmed.
According to sources, acting on a tip-off, intelligence officials learned that a passenger on a Biman Bangladesh Airlines domestic flight from Chittagong was expected to receive a gold consignment from a passenger arriving from Dubai. The domestic passenger was allegedly planning to leave the airport through the domestic terminal after collecting the gold.
Based on the intelligence, security officials intensified surveillance at the airport and identified the suspect as Mohammad Alauddin. A search led to the recovery of 720 grams of powdered gold, ingeniously concealed on his person.
Legal action has been initiated in connection with the incident.

item.title: KU students lock admin building, boycott classes over hidden camera allegation
item.description:
Khulna University (KU) students on Thursday locked the administrative building and suspended all academic activities, demanding justice over allegations that a hidden mobile phone was used to secretly record videos inside a women's dormitory washroom.
The protest erupted after residents of Bijoy ’24 Hall discovered a mobile phone concealed inside a washroom on Wednesday night.
Students subsequently detained Imam Hasan, 24, son of the hall canteen owner, who had been working at the canteen for about two years. They accused him of secretly recording videos of female students.
According to students, the phone was spotted around 10:30pm, prompting suspicion and a search. They alleged that several secretly recorded videos were found on the device.
The protesters further claimed that Imam had been recording videos through a washroom ventilator for an extended period and sharing them in various Telegram groups. They also alleged that his wife was aware of the activities.
The incident sparked outrage among residential students, who raised concerns about their privacy and safety.
Students held a protest rally at Hadi Chattar at noon, demanding a fair investigation and exemplary punishment for those responsible.
They alleged that the university administration had failed to take effective action hours after the incident came to light and claimed that previous allegations of sexual harassment involving university teachers had also not been adequately addressed.
The protesters declared that all academic and administrative activities would remain suspended until a credible investigation is completed and those responsible are brought to justice.
Bijoy ’24 Hall Provost Prof Dr Selina Ahmed said the matter is being investigated.
“The investigation is ongoing. It would not be appropriate to comment before it is completed. Necessary information and actions will be shared after the investigation report is received,” she said.

item.title: Bandarban residents risk lives crossing flood-damaged bridge
item.description:
Thousands of residents in Kuhalong Union of Bandarban Sadar are enduring severe hardship as a bridge over the Camlong stream, damaged by repeated floods, remains unsafe and unusable for vehicles.
The bridge, which first collapsed during the devastating floods of 2019, has never been fully repaired. As a result, residents—including students from at least five educational institutions—have been forced to cross the damaged structure daily, risking their lives due to the lack of an alternative route.
According to local sources, Kuhalong Union is home to more than 13,000 people. Around 5,000 residents of Camlong Para, Bhangamura Para, Barua Para, Marma Para, Dhalu Para, Chemir Mukh and Goalia Khola rely on the bridge to travel to Bandarban town and transport fruits and vegetables to markets in Chittagong and other areas.
The recent floods, triggered by days of heavy rainfall across Bandarban, have further weakened the bridge. Large sections are broken, while layers of mud deposited by floodwaters have made even pedestrian movement hazardous.
“The bridge has become a death trap. People have been suffering for years, but we have no other way to travel,” said Thuy Nu Ching Marma, a resident of Camlong area.
Local jeep driver Md Alam said the bridge had remained damaged for years and was further battered by the latest floods.
“Vehicles can no longer cross the bridge safely, disrupting transport and trade in the area,” he said.
Another resident, Md Jahangir, expressed frustration over the prolonged delay in rebuilding the bridge despite its importance to thousands of people.
Kuhalong Union Parishad Chairman Mongpu Marma said the bridge's collapse has severely disrupted the movement of people and goods. He added that the matter has repeatedly been brought to the attention of the relevant authorities.
Responding to the concerns, LGED Bandarban Executive Engineer Pratipada Dewan said a contractor has already been appointed to construct a new bridge over the Camlong stream at a cost of Tk 5 crore.
“The project has been approved and construction work will begin soon. Once completed, the new bridge will significantly improve communication and transportation in the area,” he said.

item.title: Over 800 acres of cropland in Thakurgaon remain submerged for months
item.description:
More than 800 acres of agricultural land at Salandar Farm under Thakurgaon Sugar Mill have remained submerged for nearly four months, causing extensive crop losses and pushing hundreds of farmers toward financial hardship.
Farmers say prolonged waterlogging has damaged sugarcane, potato, rice and other seasonal crops on around 814 acres of leased farmland, threatening both local livelihoods and a key source of agricultural seed production.
According to farm authorities, 33 farmers cultivated sugarcane on 239 acres this season, while another 581 acres were used for various rabi and kharif crops. Most of the affected cultivators are landless or low-income farmers who lease land from the government-owned farm through annual tenders.
Farmers estimate that sugarcane cultivation costs around Tk115,000 per acre, with many relying on loans from sugar mills and non-governmental organizations to finance production.
Lutfar Rahman, a leaseholder at the farm, said his entire sugarcane field had been ruined after remaining under water for months.
“I borrowed money to cultivate sugarcane, but the crop has rotted due to prolonged waterlogging. Now I do not know how I will repay the loans,” he said.
Many other farmers reported similar losses, saying potato fields, rice seedlings and other crops had also been destroyed.
Farmers and local residents blame the situation on a neglected drainage canal that once carried excess water from the farm to the Dhepa River. They allege that years of silt accumulation, weed growth and lack of maintenance have blocked the canal, preventing water from draining even after moderate rainfall.
“Previously, rainwater from the farm flowed into the Dhepa River through the canal. Since that connection was lost, even a small amount of rainfall causes extensive waterlogging,” said Jalal Uddin, a farmer from the Sotapir area.
Despite repeated appeals, affected farmers say no effective steps have been taken to resolve the problem.
Agricultural experts and local stakeholders warn that the impact extends beyond individual farmers. Salandar Farm supplies sugarcane to Thakurgaon Sugar Mill and produces foundation and certified seeds of crops including potato, rice, chilli and pulses for distribution across the country.
Abdul Mannan, an agriculturist and leaseholder, described the situation as a “man-made disaster”.
“Regular maintenance and re-excavation of the drainage canal could have prevented this crisis. Farmers informed the authorities long ago, but no effective action has been taken,” he said.
Farmers estimate that nearly 1,000 acres of surrounding farmland outside the farm area are also affected by waterlogging. They believe re-excavating the canal and restoring its connection to the Dhepa River could protect around 2,000 acres of fertile land and significantly increase agricultural output.
The affected farmers have submitted a memorandum to the district administration, demanding urgent excavation of the canal and immediate measures to resolve the long-standing waterlogging problem. They warn that without swift intervention, both the local sugar industry and the country's seed production network could face serious setbacks.
Former Managing Director of Thakurgaon Sugar Mill Shahjahan Kabir said the authorities are concerned about the waterlogging situation at Salandar Farm.
“We are concerned about the persistent waterlogging at Salandar Farm. Initiatives are being taken to renovate the drainage canal as quickly as possible in coordination with the Bangladesh Water Development Board and the district administration,” he said.
Acting Managing Director Saiful Islam said he had only recently assumed office.
“I have just taken charge. After reviewing the matter, I will discuss it with all relevant stakeholders and take the necessary steps,” he said.

item.title: BNP leader Rafiqul Islam Miah on life support
item.description:
BNP Standing Committee member and former minister Rafiqul Islam Miah was placed on life support at Evercare Hospital Dhaka on Thursday evening after his condition deteriorated.
He was put on life support at 7:20pm, his Personal Secretary Muksedur Rahman Abir said.
He said the BNP leader’s kidneys are no longer functioning, and doctors detected blood infection. "He has been suffering from neurological problems for a long time and is now facing multiple complications," he added.
Rafiqul Islam was admitted to Evercare Hospital on July 21 and had been receiving treatment in a cabin equipped with ICU facilities. However, his condition began to worsen from around noon on Thursday, his personal secretary said.
He is currently under the care of specialist physician Dr Farid Hossain at the hospital.
Abir said the family has sought prayers from people across the country for Rafiqul Islam's recovery.

item.title: Bangladesh expects Delhi to address peacefully protests in India
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam on Thursday said Bangladesh expects India to address promptly and peacefully the concerns of its people, being the world’s largest democracy.
"As a democratic government and state, we would expect India, as the world's largest democracy, to take into account the position of its people and move quickly towards resolving the problem," she told a media briefing at the foreign office.
The junior minister made the comments while responding to a question on the current student-led protests in the neighbouring country, adding “Bangladesh wants peace and stability to prevail in the region”.
Asked for comments on media reports about President Mohammed Shahabuddin’s alleged telephone conversation with deposed prime minister Sheikh Hasina, she said the foreign ministry had not yet any specific information on the matter.
Shama, however, said the government would investigate the matter if any relevant information became available.

item.title: Call for greater awareness to protect women's mental and physical health
item.description:
Speakers at a seminar on Saturday stressed the need to ensure women's mental and physical well-being as a prerequisite for building a healthy society, calling for greater public awareness and easier access to modern healthcare services.
The seminar, titled "Protection of Women's Mental and Physical Health," was organised by the Bangladesh Nari Sangbadik Samity (BANASAS) at the National Press Club on Wednesday.
The chief guest, Prof Dr Sheikh Nazmul Huda, chairman of the Department of Public Health at the International University of Business Agriculture and Technology (IUBAT), highlighted the indications, benefits and potential risks of Caesarean section (C-section).
He also discussed the role of political decisions and public policies in shaping healthcare services.
He said hysterectomy is not always necessary for young women suffering from conditions such as fibroids, cysts or tumours, noting that advances in modern medical treatment often make it possible to preserve the uterus while providing effective care.
Former Associate Professor of Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College and Hospital, Dr Yasmin Jahan Shaheen, called for a nationwide drive to expand cervical cancer screening, increase uptake of the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine and strengthen public awareness, warning that stigma and late diagnosis continue to claim preventable lives.
Dr Shaheen noted that cervical cancer usually develops gradually over a decade and often remains symptom-free in its early stages. She said the disease is largely preventable through HPV vaccination, ideally administered between the ages of 9 and 14, before exposure to the virus.
She added that treatment varies depending on the patient's condition and the stage of the disease, while early detection is possible through the simple Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA) screening test, which helps identify precancerous changes and enables timely treatment.
Zakia Shishir, convener of the Agrajatra Nari Forum and a human rights activist, said families and society have a critical role to play in safeguarding women's mental health, as women continue to face domestic violence, workplace harassment, social bullying and cyber abuse on a regular basis.
‘Such violence and abuse often leave women struggling with depression and psychological distress, adversely affecting their work, thinking and future aspirations. It also undermines their self-confidence, hindering both their personal and professional development.
Pharmacist and researcher Samin Fardeen Soumik delivered a presentation on osteoporosis, describing it as a "silent" bone disease that gradually weakens bones, leaving them fragile and prone to fractures from even minor falls or routine daily activities.
He said women are at greater risk of developing osteoporosis after menopause due to hormonal changes. Smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, physical inactivity and a family history of the disease are among the major risk factors.
“Osteoporosis can largely be prevented through a healthy diet, regular exercise, maintaining a healthy weight, avoiding smoking, ensuring adequate intake of calcium and vitamin D, and limiting excessive salt consumption,” he added.
Among others, Zauhar Iqbal Khan, general secretary of the Dhaka Sub-Editors Council; Shahjahan Swapan, welfare secretary of the Dhaka Union of Journalists; and Nahid Hasan, sports and cultural secretary of the Dhaka Sub-Editors Council, also addressed the seminar.
The programme was chaired by Nasima Akter Soma, President of the Bangladesh Nari Sangbadik Samity (BANASAS).

item.title: Arundhati Roy: India’s ‘Cockroach’ protest movement reflects deeper crisis in democracy
item.description:
Booker Prize-winning author and activist Arundhati Roy has described India’s emerging “Cockroach Janata Party” movement as a symbol of mounting public anger over unemployment, alleged examination paper leaks, and what she characterizes as the erosion of democratic institutions.
In an essay titled “Cockroach Democracy: Unarmed and Dangerous,” Roy argues that a student-led protest movement has grown far beyond its original demand for the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, evolving into a broader challenge to India’s political establishment.
According to Roy, the movement began after Chief Justice of India Surya Kant allegedly referred to unemployed young Indians as “cockroaches.” The remark prompted Boston-based student Abhijeet Dipke to post on Instagram, “What if all cockroaches come together?” The post quickly gained traction online, leading to the formation of what supporters call the “Cockroach Janata Party.”
Roy writes that the movement initially focused on alleged irregularities in India’s examination system, including repeated paper leaks. She cites opposition claims that more than 150 public examination papers have been leaked since 2014, devastating the prospects of millions of students.
The essay says protests intensified after Dipke returned to India and joined demonstrations at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar alongside education reform advocate Sonam Wangchuk and student activists affiliated with the All India Students Association (AISA). Roy claims the demonstrations expanded into a large march toward Parliament on July 20 despite restrictions imposed by authorities.
Describing the protests as peaceful, Roy alleges that police used force against demonstrators, including baton charges and tear gas, while protesters continued marching toward Parliament. She argues that the government’s response exposed what she calls an increasingly authoritarian approach to dissent.
Roy further contends that the movement has united people across religious, caste, and class divisions and has become a wider expression of frustration over unemployment, inflation, environmental disputes, and citizenship-related policies.
In the essay, she also raises concerns about the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), the National Register of Citizens (NRC), and the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, arguing that these measures have intensified uncertainty over citizenship and voting rights for many Indians.
The author claims India’s democratic institutions including the Election Commission, judiciary, police, and sections of the media have become increasingly compromised, allegations that have been repeatedly rejected by the Indian government.
While acknowledging that the movement may not immediately lead to political change, Roy argues that it reflects growing public dissatisfaction and could mark an important moment in India’s contemporary political history.
She concludes by warning that tensions could escalate if authorities respond with further force, while urging citizens and opposition parties to build on what she describes as a rare display of youth-led civic mobilization.

item.title: The sculpting matriarchs: A final-day visit to the Novera Ahmed retrospective
item.description:
When I first learned from a social media post that a special exhibition dedicated to the works of Bangladesh’s pioneer sculptor Novera Ahmed was underway at our national museum—running from July 4 to 21—I decided almost immediately that it was a must-visit.
By the time I found out about the exhibition, titled “Novera, নভেরা ,” it was already more than halfway through. Unfortunately, I initially picked a Thursday to visit, only to discover it was the museum's weekly day off. Finally, I managed to get a close look at her masterpieces on display at the Nalini Kanta Bhattasali Exhibition Gallery of the Bangladesh National Museum on the final day of the show, July 21st.
The writer looking at a display panel at an exhibition on Novera Ahmed’s works at Bangladesh National Museum. The historical black-and-white archival photograph in the background depicts Novera Ahmed herself at work, painting on a large canvas. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
It was truly rewarding, particularly for someone like me who never had the chance to meet this preeminent sculptor during her lifetime, but whose generation has always been deeply appreciative of her. Novera remains an immense source of inspiration for subsequent generations of artists, not just for her creations, but for her radical spirit. For too long, Novera Ahmed and her works remained shrouded in mystery—partly due to her long absence from Bangladesh and extended stay abroad, and partly because of a historical lack of public understanding regarding an art form that the vast majority of people were unfamiliar with in the 1950s, 60s, and 70s.
Interestingly, Novera belonged to a matriarchal generation of sculptors. In a league of her own alongside Rabia Zuberi, Meera Mukherjee, and Pilloo Pochkhanawala, these all-female artistic pathfinders of British India pioneered modern sculpting across the geographical territories of today's Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India. Novera Ahmed single-handedly introduced modernist, three-dimensional sculpting into East Pakistan.
Novera Ahmed`s famous masterpiece, `Cow with Two Figures` on display at the Bangladesh National Museum. Sculpted in cement in 1958, this iconic artwork is widely celebrated as the first-ever open-air public sculpture created in Bangladesh (then East Pakistan). Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
Born in 1939 in the Sundarbans region due to the professional posting of her father, Syed Ahmed, her ancestral home was actually in North Para, Askar Dighi, Chittagong. She spent her childhood in Kolkata, matriculating from the Loreto School there. Following the partition of the subcontinent, she moved to East Pakistan with her family in 1947, studying first at Comilla Victoria College and later at Chittagong College.
While Novera was transforming herself into a trailblazing sculptor in East Pakistan and traveling widely through the capital cities of Southeast Asia and Europe, a few other female artists were also making their names by introducing modern sculpture to India and Pakistan. Often hailed as the "Queen Mother of Arts" and Pakistan's first professional female sculptor, Rabia Zuberi (1940–2022) was a massive institutional and creative force in Pakistani art. Meanwhile, artists like Pilloo Pochkhanawala (1923–1986), Meera Mukherjee (1923–1998), and Leela Mukherjee (1916–2002) were busy introducing modern sculpting to India.
Novera Ahmed’s poignant sculptural masterpiece, `Mother and Children`, on display at the Bangladesh National Museum. Cast in cement, this piece forms a core part of Novera`s highly acclaimed Family Series. It deeply explores the universal themes of maternal love, rural motherhood, and ancestral roots. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
Among this small crowd of the subcontinent’s first-generation modern female sculptors, our very own Novera Ahmed stood out in many respects. She blended Western avant-garde styles (heavily influenced by Henry Moore) with local folk traditions and rural themes. Her work focused on geometric, anthropomorphic human and animal forms, particularly themes of womanhood. Novera, who studied sculpture at the Camberwell School of Arts and Crafts in London from 1951 to 1955 under the tutelage of the eminent Czech sculptor Dr. Karel Vogel, achieved a National Diploma in Design.
She received further training in Florence from Venturino Venturi, and went on to produce East Pakistan’s first frieze on the wall of the Central Public Library in 1957, as well as its first open-air sculpture, Cow with Two Figures , in 1958.
A dark-patina piece from Novera Ahmed`s iconic Family Series on display at the exhibition. This piece presents a highly stylized, abstract interpretation of a family unit. It features an elongated, central parental figure cradling a tiny child on its shoulder, flanked by a smaller accompanying figure to the lower left. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
In August 1960, she held her first solo exhibition, Inner Gaze , in Dhaka, showcasing 75 exhibits executed mainly in cement between 1956 and 1960. This was likely the first-ever solo sculpture exhibition by any sculptor in Bangladesh. Novera also assisted Hamidur Rahman in designing the initial artistic layout of the iconic Central Shaheed Minar monument, though work was temporarily suspended when martial law was imposed in 1958. That same year, she installed the outdoor courtyard sculpture Cow and Two Figures at the residence of an industrialist in the Tejgaon industrial area.
After her historic 1960 exhibition at the Central Public Library—held under the joint aegis of the Pakistan United Nations Association and the Asia Foundation—Novera traveled to Lahore at the invitation of the renowned poet Faiz Ahmed Faiz. There, her sculpture Child Philosopher won first prize at the All Pakistan Painting and Sculpture Exhibition in 1961. She subsequently traveled extensively through India, Myanmar, Thailand, Hong Kong, France, Greece, Italy, and Switzerland, bridging South Asian heritage with global avant-garde art movements.
Two striking, heavily textured bronze miniature sculptures from Novera Ahmed’s later artistic periods, on display at the retrospective exhibition. These pieces present elongated, highly stylized human figures – one female and another male. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
During her travels through Thailand, Japan, Malaysia, and Laos in 1968, she witnessed the horrors of the Vietnam War. Consequently, for a 1970 exhibition in Bangkok, she constructed 11 monumental sculptures using aluminum scraps recovered from crashed US military warplanes. This process of transforming instruments of destruction into expressions of creativity carried a profound pacifist and non-violent message. By the end of that year, she permanently relocated to Paris.
Following a successful sculpture exhibition in Paris in 1973, she entered a period of self-imposed exile, dedicating the remainder of her life primarily to painting rather than sculpture. In 1975, Novera survived a severe road accident in Paris that left her with permanent leg injuries, causing her to walk with a limp for the rest of her life. She suffered a stroke in 2013 and passed away in a Paris hospital on May 6, 2015.
Two striking, heavily textured bronze miniature sculptures from Novera Ahmed’s later artistic periods, on display at the retrospective exhibition. These pieces present elongated, highly stylized human figures – one female and another male. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
The exhibition that rounded off in Dhaka on July 21st gave me a rare opportunity to time-travel through Novera’s life journey by admiring her legendary works. The gallery was beautifully arranged with sculptures on white plinths, biographical panels spread across the walls, and a glass case containing her garments and personal belongings, giving visitors a direct, intimate sense of the artist’s presence alongside her creative history.
The show offered a unique opportunity for the new generation to rediscover a legendary artist who profoundly shaped the history of modern sculpture in Pakistan and Bangladesh. Bangladesh has since honored her memory and contributions by bestowing upon her both the Ekushey Padak and the Independence Award.
The image shows Novera balanced on a wooden ladder, actively modeling and refining a large-scale, texture-heavy plaster or concrete structure. This piece belongs to her prolific late 1950s period in Dhaka, where she worked long hours in her studio to prepare for her historic first solo exhibition in 1960. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
Across the Indian subcontinent, the introduction and popularization of modern sculpture were pioneered by extraordinary, trailblazing women who shattered deep-seated social taboos in a heavily male-dominated field. As one of the premier pioneering forces of this movement, Novera’s legacy will continue to inspire a new breed of sculptors in our part of the world. The revolution Novera Ahmed carved into stone, wood, and cement will remain an eternal source of inspiration for today’s youth and progressive artists worldwide.
A glass display vitrine containing personal artifacts belonging to Novera Ahmed, showcased as part of the biographical section of her retrospective exhibition. These include carefully folded garments—such as a traditional green-and-red patterned saree—and a pair of well-worn, patterned fabric indoor slippers. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune

BLAST submits recommendations to amend labor rules
item.description:
The Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (BLAST) has submitted recommendations to amend the Bangladesh Labor Rules, 2015 to the Ministry of Labor and Employment and the relevant committee to strengthen workers' rights and improve workplace safety and access to justice. The recommendations were sent to the ministry on July 22, 2026, and to the committee on July 23, 2026.
The recommendations were prepared in line with the Bangladesh Labor Act, 2006, as amended in 2026, international labor standards and workers' practical experiences.
BLAST proposed measures to strengthen workplace safety, prevent violence and harassment, and improve access to justice in labor courts. The organization recommended introducing provisions for safe work practices, regular risk assessments and mandatory occupational health and safety training for all workers.
It also recommended incorporating clear provisions, responsibilities and implementation procedures for the compensation fund established under the law for workplace deaths and injuries.
BLAST welcomed the inclusion of key High Court directives in the latest amendment to the Bangladesh Labor Act, 2006. However, it recommended explicitly including cyber harassment within the definition of sexual harassment, citing growing risks of technology-based harassment in workplaces.
The organization also proposed establishing a clear, effective and accountable mechanism for receiving, investigating and resolving complaints related to workplace violence, harassment and discrimination.
BLAST Director (Law) Md Barkat Ali said: “Necessary amendments to the Labor Rules are essential for the effective implementation of the latest amendment to the Bangladesh Labor Act, 2006. The rights recognized in the Domestic Workers Protection and Welfare Policy, 2015 need to be incorporated into the Labor Rules. Initiatives such as including cyber harassment in the definition of sexual harassment, effectively implementing the workplace accident compensation fund and introducing paralegal services in labor courts will further strengthen the protection of workers' rights and access to justice.”
To improve legal assistance and alternative dispute resolution for workers, BLAST also recommended introducing paralegal services in labor courts.
BLAST said it hopes the recommendations will be considered during the amendment process to strengthen workers' rights, improve workplace safety and accountability, expand access to justice and make the labor dispute resolution system more effective and accessible.

ICT compulsory, but treachers of other subjects teach it
item.description:
Information and Communication Technology (ICT) became a compulsory subject at the secondary and higher secondary levels 13 years ago. However, the necessary teaching posts were not created when the subject was introduced, nor was recruitment coordinated accordingly.

As a result, many government colleges still do not have their own ICT teachers, while not a single government secondary school in the country has a separate teaching post for the subject.

Teachers of physics, zoology or other subjects are taking ICT classes in many government colleges. Elsewhere, programmers, guest teachers or part-time teachers are conducting the lessons. In government secondary schools, trained teachers of mathematics, business studies and science rotate to teach the subject.

The crisis in ICT education has become even more evident at a time when Bangladesh lags behind several neighbouring countries in international indices of digital development.

According to the latest data from the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), only 53.4 per cent of the country's population uses the internet.

Although network coverage has expanded, the meaningful use of technology in education, public services, financial transactions and employment remains limited.

Teachers and educationists said that although ICT is a practical skills-based subject, regular practical classes are not held in many institutions because of the shortage of teachers.

As a result, students remain confined to exam-oriented learning instead of acquiring the digital skills they need. They believe that without ensuring effective ICT education in educational institutions, it will be difficult to reduce the country's digital skills gap.

In line with the National Education Policy 2010, ICT was made compulsory at the secondary and higher secondary levels in 2013. Since then, students have been taking the subject in the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) and Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) examinations.

However, the crisis has persisted because the subject was introduced without the necessary preparation in terms of creating teaching posts and recruiting teachers.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, Director General of the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE), Professor Khan Moinuddin Al Mahmud Sohel, said: "There is a shortage of teachers in various subjects, including ICT, in government secondary schools and government colleges. DSHE has sent proposals to the Ministry of Education for recruiting teachers based on the required posts and staffing needs. The ministry has forwarded the proposals to the Bangladesh Public Service Commission (PSC). We hope the crisis will largely be resolved once the recruitment process is completed."

However, proposals from DSHE for creating new teaching posts often remain stuck in the ministry for a long time due to bureaucratic delays.

First recruitment after eight years, but no continuity

According to the Ministry of Education and the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE), there are currently 708 government colleges in the country. Of these, 691 offer higher secondary education.

Among the 345 older colleges that became government institutions by 2000, 65 still do not have ICT teaching posts. However, 17 of them have lecturer posts in Computer Education.

Another 363 colleges were nationalised under the 2018 regulations. Of these, 102 still do not have ICT teaching posts.

Even where posts have been created, they have not all been filled. According to DSHE, a total of 255 cadre posts for ICT lecturers—one in each government college—were created in 2016. Later, another 18 cadre posts were added.

Through the 38th Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) examination, 145 ICT lecturers joined government colleges for the first time in 2021. In other words, subject-specific teacher recruitment began nearly eight years after ICT became a compulsory subject. Of them, 132 are currently serving.

The ICT posts in colleges nationalised under the 2018 regulations are non-cadre positions. As a result, teachers belonging to the BCS Education Cadre cannot join these posts. Consequently, many colleges continue to rely on teachers from other subjects, guest teachers or part-time teachers to teach ICT.

According to the recommendations of the Enam Committee on administrative reform, each subject at the degree and higher secondary levels should have at least one associate professor, one assistant professor and two lecturers. However, this structure has not been established for ICT in most colleges.

Even after the first recruitment, appointments have not continued regularly. Through the 45th, 46th, 47th and 49th Special BCS examinations, the Bangladesh Public Service Commission (PSC) has recommended a total of 103 ICT lecturers. However, they have yet to join their respective posts.

Meanwhile, the National University has decided to make ICT compulsory in several years of undergraduate studies. People concerned believe that unless the required number of teachers is recruited, this new initiative will also face implementation challenges.

No posts in government schools

The situation at the secondary level is even more alarming. According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Educational Information and Statistics (BANBEIS), there are 702 government secondary schools in the country. These schools have 15,293 approved posts for assistant teachers, of which more than 3,000 remain vacant. Another 383 headteacher posts are also vacant.

Yet, even 13 years after ICT became a compulsory subject, not a single separate teaching post has been created for ICT in government secondary schools. As a result, teachers of mathematics, business studies and science, after receiving training or when necessary, take ICT classes.

DSHE has recently sent a proposal to the Ministry of Education to create 872 ICT teacher posts. The proposal includes one ICT teacher post each for 532 single-shift schools and two ICT teacher posts each for 170 double-shift schools.

Although teacher recruitment at the secondary level is subject-based, the recruitment process is lengthy. A DSHE official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that once ICT teaching posts are created, steps should be taken to recruit teachers quickly through a special arrangement.

Scenario from two institutions

Dhaka College has around 2,400 students in Classes XI and XII. Yet, even 13 years after ICT became compulsory, the college does not have a single ICT teacher from the BCS Education Cadre.

A visit to the college on 19 July found that teachers of physics, zoology and other subjects were taking ICT classes. In addition, two computer programmers who had worked under an expired postgraduate-level project are also involved in teaching. Their salaries are paid from non-government sources.

Professor Abul Hasnat Masum Iqbal of the Physics Department, who is currently in charge of the ICT Department, told Prothom Alo that considering the number of students, the college needs at least two permanent ICT teachers of its own.

Motijheel Government Boys' High School also has no separate ICT teacher post. Several teachers at the school said that trained teachers of physics, mathematics and other subjects teach ICT. One of them said he himself had previously taught the subject to students in Classes VII and VIII.

The teachers said that because of the shortage of staff, it is not possible to conduct ICT practical classes regularly.

Same crisis outside Dhaka

Netrokona Government Women's College has around 2,000 students in Classes XI and XII. However, the college has only one government-appointed ICT teacher. Principal Md Gias Uddin told Prothom Alo that although ICT is compulsory for all students, it is impossible for a single teacher to take regular classes for so many students. As a result, the college has appointed a guest teacher to continue teaching the subject. Several students also said their ICT classes are not held regularly because of the shortage of teachers.

The situation is the same at Netrokona Government College. The college has around 2,600 students in Classes XI and XII but only one government-appointed ICT teacher.

Promotion bottleneck

Government colleges are facing not only a shortage of ICT teachers but also limited opportunities for promotion. A proposal to create 291 ICT posts—from lecturer to professor—in 51 government colleges has remained pending at the Ministry of Education for a long time. As a result, many teachers recruited through the 38th BCS examination have become eligible for promotion to assistant professor but cannot be promoted because higher-level posts have not been created.

An engineering degree in the relevant discipline is mandatory for appointment as an ICT lecturer. At present, around 50 ICT lecturers serving in government colleges are graduates of engineering universities, including BUET, KUET, RUET and CUET. In the latest 49th Special BCS examination, about 22,500 candidates applied for just 25 ICT lecturer posts.

In other words, there is no shortage of qualified candidates. Rather, the crisis has become prolonged because of the failure to create the required posts, recruit teachers regularly and establish a proper promotion structure.

Asked, SM Hafizur Rahman, a professor at the Institute of Education and Research at the University of Dhaka, told Prothom Alo that information technology is evolving rapidly, and ICT textbooks have been revised to keep pace with those changes.

However, he said it would be difficult to implement the revisions effectively in classrooms without teachers who specialise in ICT. He stressed that the shortage of ICT teachers in schools and colleges must be addressed promptly to ensure the successful implementation of the updated curriculum.

Prothom Alo's Netrokona Correspondent contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump imposes forced labor duties on 60 trading partners as 10pc US tariffs expire
item.description:
USA-TRUMP/

The Trump administration on Friday imposed new tariffs of 10 per cent and 12.5 per cent on goods from 60 trading partners, including the European Union and China, over allegations of lax enforcement of forced labor bans, just as a temporary 10 per cent global tariff expired.

The move is the White House's latest effort to restore President Donald Trump's campaign vision of a near-global tariff after the US Supreme Court in February struck down his "reciprocal" duties of 10 per cent to 50 per cent imposed last year under a national emergencies law to try to shrink the US trade deficit.

The new tariffs, announced on Thursday in a Federal Register notice, cover 99.4 per cent of US imports, but include numerous product exemptions, such as oil and gas, fertilizer and certain food items.

Imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, the new duties allow the administration to maintain a tariff floor on virtually all US imports despite the Supreme Court setback. The tariffs are also likely to face less legal risk than those struck down in February, as Section 301 has survived prior court challenges.

Trump's temporary 10 per cent global tariff expired at 12:01 am EDT on Friday (0401 GMT) after 150 days. The new duties took effect at that exact same moment, with goods in transit exempted until 12:01 am EDT on 28 July.

"The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it. It’s well past time for our trading partners to do the same," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement. "Today’s action will begin to correct what is both a human rights abuse and distortive trade practice to improve the welfare of workers everywhere."

Greer has previously pledged that for countries that have reached trade deals with Washington capping US tariff rates, the new forced labor duties would not push them above those caps.

The US imposed a 10 per cent duty on goods of Argentina, Bangladesh, Britain, Cambodia, Canada, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Mexico, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago.

The European Union, Taiwan, Japan, South Korea and Switzerland were assigned rates that, combined with pre-existing most-favored-nation tariff rates, totaled 10 per cent or 12.5 per cent.

US trade deal: Trump imposes new tariffs, what’s ahead for Bangladesh

The other 38 countries were assigned a 12.5 per cent rate. These include Vietnam, which issued a new decree this week that sets out more detailed rules banning imports of goods made with forced labor, and China - accused by the US of detaining Uyghur minorities in work camps, which Beijing denies.

Trump administration officials have told Chinese counterparts they intend to rebuild Trump's second-term tariffs on Chinese goods back up to the 20 per cent that was agreed upon in a trade truce with Chinese President Xi Jinping in November 2025 - but not exceed that level. Prior to Friday's action, China's tariff rate had fallen to 10 per cent, excluding the 25 per cent imposed during Trump's first term on industrial goods.

Countries Protest

The action drew immediate protests from some trade partners. European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc viewed the new tariffs as a shock and Washington's rationale did not make sense.

"If you compare our labor laws to the ones of the United States, I mean, we have paid vacations, we have very good labor conditions for our employees, so it's not really grounded," she told Reuters on the sidelines of ASEAN meetings in Manila.

Australia and Brazil described the new tariffs as unjustified and said they would seek to have them removed, while Norway said there was "no basis" for them.

Canada - hit on Monday with new Trump tariffs on USD 20 billion worth of goods - issued a muted response to the "unilateral" tariffs.

"We will continue engaging constructively with the United States on this matter, as well as other outstanding issues, over the coming weeks to the mutual benefit of our citizens," said Dominic LeBlanc, Canada's minister in charge of US trade.

Kelly Ann Shaw, a former White House trade adviser in Trump's first term and a partner with the Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld law firm, said the new tariffs closely tracked what had been telegraphed, although some changes had been made, including the addition of some 471 products to an exclusion list.

"I think this is more status quo in terms of the economic impact," she said. Partners including the EU had negotiated tariff caps, which meant their new tariffs would be lower than under their earlier agreement, she said.

A senior Trump administration official disputed suggestions that the forced labor tariffs were simply a direct replacement for the expiring levies despite the timing, similar duty rates and vast coverage of nearly all US imports.

Trump’s special envoy due in Dhaka to sound out Bangladesh’s foreign policy direction

The official said the US has stronger import bans on goods made with forced labor and enforces them more rigidly than any other country, giving rivals an unfair trading advantage over the US.

Both Democrats and Republicans in Congress have been calling for the eradication of forced labor from global supply chains, "so we're really responding to that call," the official said.

Ryan Majerus, a trade lawyer and former Commerce Department official, said the new tariffs could be harder to challenge in court because Section 301 has withstood past challenges and some judges may be reluctant to enjoin actions to curb forced labor.

"Once the 301 duties are placed, they have a lot of flexibility to adjust them," said Majerus, a partner at King and Spalding. "It's a sledgehammer. It's also intended to keep the ...10 per cent baseline in place, and they think they're well protected when this goes to court."

Many goods will be exempted from the duties, including oil and gas, fertilizer, certain foodstuffs and goods that are already subject to Section 232 national security tariffs, such as autos, steel, aluminum and copper, the official said. Aircraft and parts will also be exempted, along with critical minerals.

Other goods that comply with the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement on trade will also be exempted because of the highly integrated North American supply chain and high levels of US content in these products.
